persona.name: Priya
persona.profile: Two years, almost all of it React and Node front-end work; this is her first low-level design exercise. Models the nouns from the problem statement as classes with fields, getters and setters, and connects them the way the sentences in the brief connect them. Walkthroughs are honest but sketchy — she is not sure which object should own which decision, and says so in her assumptions.

designReport:
Report for the design stage (overall so far 2.7):
- requirement-coverage: 3/4 — 1 of 6 requirements have nothing in the design that speaks to them: "Entry is refused when no suitable spot is free". Suggestion: Add a class that owns each missing requirement, or state in your assumptions why it is out of scope.
- class-responsibilities: 2/4 — ParkingLot lists 3 separate responsibilities in one sentence: "Manages floors and overall entry/exit workflow". Suggestion: Split ParkingLot. Pull out the responsibility with the fewest dependencies on the rest — usually calculation rather than coordination.
- coupling-cohesion: 3/4 — VehicleType is declared but connected to nothing — usually a noun taken from the brief before deciding what it does. Suggestion: Either connect each orphan to the classes that use it, or drop it.
- abstraction-use: 1/4 — pricing strategy has no interface or abstract type. It currently lives inside RateTable, so rate rules change constantly in the real world — hourly, daily cap, weekend, ev, validation stamps means editing that class every time. spot allocation strategy has no interface or abstract type. It currently lives inside Ticket, so nearest-to-entrance, floor-fill, and reserved-first are all legitimate and swappable means editing that class every time. Suggestion: Introduce an interface for pricing strategy and move the varying behaviour behind it.
- behaviour: 4/4 — All 3 scenarios walked, every step lands on a declared class and method, and the work is spread across 5 classes. The refusal path is traced explicitly. Suggestion: Keep walkthroughs alongside the design as it grows; they are the cheapest test you have.
- edge-cases: 3/4 — The design mentions a refusal in the walkthrough, but the refusal is handled implicitly (e.g., returning null or skipping ticket creation) rather than as an explicit domain concept. Suggestion: Model the refusal as a distinct result type or exception (e.g., EntryDenied) that callers must handle, and document this as an explicit assumption.

rationale: I added a ChargingSpot subclass with a ChargingSession to capture kWh usage, introduced PricingStrategy (and concrete TimeBasedPricing & ChargingPricing) so EV billing can be per‑kWh, and created SpotAllocationStrategy to separate spot‑choice logic. EntryResult now carries either a Ticket or a ChargingSpot plus a status enum, making the refusal case explicit rather than implicit. These changes keep EV concerns isolated while addressing the tool's feedback on abstraction, coupling, and explicit refusal handling.
changeReport:
Report for the change stage (overall so far 2.7):
- change-resilience: 3/4 — Added ChargingSpot, ChargingSession, ElectricCar, EntryResult, EntryStatus, PricingStrategy, TimeBasedPricing, ChargingPricing, SpotAllocationStrategy, FirstFitAllocation behind Vehicle, which already existed. 5 existing classes were reopened: ParkingLot (responsibility, attributes, methods); Spot (responsibility); Vehicle (attributes); Ticket (responsibility); VehicleType (attributes). Suggestion: Reduce the wiring: only one existing class should need to know ChargingSpot exists.

Mentor's note: The main wiring problem is that every existing class now has to know about ChargingSpot – ParkingLot, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket and VehicleType all reference it. This tight coupling makes the design brittle and hard to extend; if you add another EV feature you’ll have to touch many places.

p-pricing.text: Weekend rates start next month. Which method in RateTable changes, and which other classes have to know about it?

The only thing that would actually change in the model is **RateTable** – we’d add a new method (or overload `getRate`) that takes a date/DayOfWeek and returns the weekend rate, or we could add a `weekendRates` map and a `getWeekendRate(vehicleType)` helper.

The only other classes that need to know about that change are the ones that call the table: **TimeBasedPricing** (its `calculate` method will now ask for the weekend rate when the entry/exit date falls on Saturday/Sunday) and, indirectly, any code that builds or injects the `PricingStrategy` (e.g., the `ParkingLot` constructor). No other domain objects need to be touched.
How will the ParkingLot constructor adapt to use the new RateTable method that returns a weekend rate?

p-split.text: ParkingLot describes more than one job. If you had to split it into two classes tonight, where is the cut — and which of the two does Ticket talk to?

I’d pull the “entry/exit workflow” out of ParkingLot into a new **GateController** (or EntryExitService). ParkingLot would then only own the physical layout (floors → spots) and the strategy look‑ups. GateController would orchestrate the ticket creation, spot lookup via the allocation strategy, and call back to ParkingLot to mark a spot occupied/vacant. So when a car comes in, GateController asks ParkingLot for a spot, builds the Ticket and returns an EntryResult. On exit GateController reads the Ticket (or EntryResult), asks the appropriate PricingStrategy, then tells ParkingLot to release the spot. Thus Ticket is owned/handled by the **GateController**, not directly by ParkingLot.

p-spot-size.text: Spot size and vehicle size: are they a value, an enum, or a class hierarchy in your design? What would make you change that choice?

In my sketch I treated both as enums (SpotSize = SMALL/MEDIUM/LARGE and VehicleType = MOTORCYCLE/CAR/TRUCK/ELECTRIC_CAR). That works for a simple hierarchy where “size” is just a comparable label and we only need a size‑check (`canFit`).  

If we later need richer semantics – e.g. different dimensions per model, weight limits, or dynamic spot‑reconfiguration – I’d promote SpotSize (and maybe VehicleSize) to a value object class with fields like length, width, height, maxWeight, plus a `fits(SpotSize)` method. The enum would then just expose predefined instances. This gives us flexibility without breaking existing code, at the cost of a little more boilerplate.

defendReport:
Report for the defend stage (overall so far 2.7):

Mentor's note: Add a dedicated place in the design document where each decision lists its rejected alternatives and the conditions that would trigger a redesign. For example, explain why FirstFitAllocation was chosen over a floor‑fill or reserved strategy and under what traffic patterns that choice might shift. This explicit trade‑off mapping will make the ParkingLot and SpotAllocationStrategy more robust and easier to evolve as demand or pricing models change.

exit.q1: Yeah, the feedback about the missing entry‑refusal requirement was a wake‑up – I hadn’t realized I hadn’t modeled that as a concrete domain concept, I was just returning null somewhere.
exit.q2: I disagreed with the coupling‑cohesion comment that every class must know about ChargingSpot; I thought it was okay because the lot needs to know which spots are charging‑compatible, but the reviewer is right that it adds unnecessary wiring.
exit.q3: I would tell a friend to use this as a cautionary example – it shows how easy it is to forget edge cases and over‑couple new features, but also how valuable quick walkthroughs and explicit result types are for a solid low‑level design.
